Delusion
dē-lū´zhŭn
n. (a deception believed; a false persuasion sent or permitted as judgment; rendering Greek plane and Hebrew ta'alul)
Latin deludere, to play false, to mock — de, thoroughly, and ludere, to play. A delusion is not merely an error but an error the man is being played with.

Biblical Definition

“And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie: That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness” (2Th 2:11–12) — and the cause is given in the verse before, that they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. Isaiah says the same of those who chose their own ways: “I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears upon them; because when I called, none did answer” (Isa 66:4). James warns the church: “be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jas 1:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines delusion as the act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind; false representation; illusion; error or mistake proceeding from false views.

expand to see more

DELUSION, n. The act of deluding; deception; a misleading of the mind.

2. False representation; illusion; error or mistake proceeding from false views.

3. A false belief; a fixed persuasion of what is not real.

Key Scripture

2Th 2:11 — "And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie:"

2Th 2:12 — "That they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness."

Isa 66:4 — "I also will choose their delusions, and will bring their fears upon them; because when I called, none did answer; when I spake, they did not hear: but they did evil before mine eyes, and chose that in which I delighted not."

Jas 1:22 — "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."

2Th 2:10 — "And with all deceivableness of unrighteousness in them that perish; because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved."

Modern Corruption

Unbelief is treated as an intellectual misfortune, and Paul makes the delusion a judgment on a prior refusal of the love of the truth.

expand to see more

Second Thessalonians 2:10–12 gives the sequence in three steps, and the order is the doctrine. First, they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved — a refusal, and note that it is the love of the truth, not merely its information; a man may hold the truth accurately and not love it. Second, for this cause God shall send them strong delusion. Third, that they all might be damned who believed not the truth, but had pleasure in unrighteousness. The delusion is not the cause of the unbelief. It is the punishment of it, and it is sent.

This is the hardest form of judgment in Scripture, because it is invisible to the man under it. Romans 1 has the same shape in the phrase God gave them over; Isaiah 66:4 has it in I also will choose their delusions. A God who abandons a man to what he wanted is doing something more terrible than striking him, and it leaves no mark the sufferer can feel. The pastoral use of the doctrine is not to identify who is under it — nobody can — but to explain why arguing is often useless, and why the prayer for an unbeliever must ask for something deeper than persuasion.

James 1:22 keeps the doctrine from being aimed only at outsiders. The hearer of the word who is not a doer is deceiving his own self — the same family of words, and here the deceiver and the deceived are one man. That delusion is self-administered and is the commonest in the church: it needs no false teacher, only a regular attendance and a settled habit of not doing anything about what is heard, and it produces a man who believes he stands where he does not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek plane (G4106), a wandering, error, delusion; energeia planes, a working of error; paralogizomai (G3884), to deceive by reasoning; Hebrew ta'alul (H8586), a caprice, delusion.

expand to see more

Greek plane (G4106) — error, delusion; 2 Thessalonians 2:11, Ephesians 4:14, 1 John 4:6, Jude 1:11.

Greek paralogizomai (G3884) — to deceive, delude by false reasoning; James 1:22, Colossians 2:4.

Hebrew ta'alul (H8586) — delusion, caprice; Isaiah 66:4, 3:4.

Usage

"“God shall send them strong delusion” — the punishment of a prior refusal, not its cause."

"“I also will choose their delusions” — because when I called, none did answer."

"“Deceiving your own selves” — the delusion that needs no false teacher."
